source.title: Temporal Scaling Law for Large Language Models
source.authors: Yizhe Xiong; Xiansheng Chen; Xin Ye; Hui Chen; Zijia Lin; Haoran Lian; Zhenpeng Su; Wei Huang; Jianwei Niu; Jungong Han; Guiguang Ding

record.file_problem: Full paper and appendices are present. Minor text-extraction and formatting artifacts do not prevent reading.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares a power-law fit with other fits for held-out loss over a model's training progress and reports that the power law is not sufficiently precise for that temporal trajectory.
record.gate_note: The measured power-law fit is for loss over training progress on a fixed model, not the usual cross-model scaling of final loss with parameters, data scale, or compute. The paper also reports same-model early-to-late prediction results, data-mixture selection and downstream scores, and position-wise loss results; these do not test the corresponding claim versions. Cited results from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study fits loss against training progress inside single fixed-size runs with a cosine learning-rate schedule. It does not measure final loss across separately trained models varying parameters, tokens or compute. The authors call this a complementary temporal law, not a test of prior scaling laws. Its power-law comparison is a baseline for its own method on a different construct: a within-run, schedule-shaped trajectory. It is therefore recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a test of V1 or V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also state that a whole-loss power-law fit over training steps is 'not precise enough' for the temporal trajectory. They also say the temporal law complements prior scaling laws, which govern final loss versus budget, rather than contradicting them.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits and predicts loss over training progress for a given model, including token-position losses. It does not fit final losses across model sizes, training-data sizes, or compute budgets as in the original scaling-law method.
record.method_sensitivity: Fit form changes the reported fit quality: the paper compares power-law whole-loss fits with its temporal law and compares several functions for token-position and temporal-parameter fits. It also reports that the a2 temporal pattern correlates with the learning-rate schedule.

fits_no_version.finding: A single power law L=(p1 x)^p2+p3, fitted to the whole held-out loss trajectory of one cosine-schedule run, gives R² 0.63–0.77 (9.8M and 58M models, ID-Val and OOD-Val). The authors' token-position temporal law gives R² >0.98. Early-to-late prediction with power-law baselines also has much larger MSE for the 468M–6.7B models (e.g. R² −1.26 vs 0.87 at 10% of training for the 1.2B model). The trajectory's converging term tracks the learning-rate schedule.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within a single pretraining run with a decaying LR schedule, loss over training steps is not well described by a single power law; its shape follows the LR schedule.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The power-law comparison concerns temporal trajectories at fixed model sizes and a particular training setup, rather than independently varying parameter count, data scale, or compute. The study reports only two models in the Table 2 comparison.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 3 and 5 report same-model early-to-late loss prediction against baselines, not small-run-to-large-run extrapolation. Tables 4 and 5 report outcomes of data-mixture selection, including downstream benchmark scores, rather than downstream scaling with model scale or pretraining loss. Position-wise loss fits and weighting-strategy results do not measure the claim's parameter/token/compute scaling relations.

untested.parts: Final held-out loss versus parameters, tokens or compute across separately trained models is never fitted. The 9.8M–6.7B models are not used for a size-scaling fit.
Nothing is extrapolated from small runs to larger runs. Prediction is early-to-late within the same model.
There is no compute-optimal allocation analysis.
There is no comparison of shape at a fixed parameter count.
Downstream scores are reported only for data-mixture choices, not as a function of scale or loss.
There is no analysis of how cross-model exponents or the compute-optimal split depend on setup or fitting choices.

missing.what: Early-to-late prediction MSE and R² for the power-law, reciprocal and logarithmic baselines versus the temporal law. Relevant only to the fits_no_version finding, not to any version.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's labels are rejected: 'challenges' V1 and 'supports' V7. Both rest on rows measuring within-run learning curves under a cosine schedule, which V1 and V7 do not name. The power-law misfit is plausibly driven by the LR schedule, since a2 tracks the cosine. The rows also compare the study's own method against a baseline. Kaplan did fit L(N,S) learning curves, but V1 as stated concerns scaling across runs. A curator who treats learning curves as covered by V1 could revisit this, but the cosine-schedule confound would still make the result weak evidence.

versions.untested_parts: Tests loss over training progress with model size and training setup fixed; does not independently test final loss scaling with parameter count, total dataset size, or compute across several orders of magnitude.
The study predicts later loss on the same target model from its early training data, not losses of much larger runs from fits to smaller runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split is tested.
No comparison of depth, width, or architecture details at fixed parameter count for this claim.
The reported experiments concern text pretraining; no other modality, repeated-data regime, fine-tuning, or transfer scaling law is tested.
The paper reports downstream benchmark scores for data-mixture choices, but does not test whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale or pretraining loss.

The study compares fit forms for temporal loss trajectories, but does not test how published cross-model exponents or compute-optimal splits vary with parameter counting, data, schedules, or other setup choices.

rows.subject: 9.8M
rows.operation_detail: Fit a power law to the whole held-out test-loss trajectory over training tokens and report R².
rows.measure: R² for power-law fit to whole test loss over training progress
rows.note: The paper describes the whole-trajectory power-law fit as not precise enough; the temporal-law value is the reported comparison.
rows.check: Measures the R² of a power law fitted to one run's loss over training steps under a cosine schedule. V1 concerns final loss across runs scaled in N, D or C, so this measure cannot show V1's effect. The baseline is the authors' own temporal law, which makes this a method-versus-baseline comparison.

rows.check: Same issue as r1, on OOD-Val: a within-run trajectory fit with the authors' method as baseline. It does not bear on cross-run scaling.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Whole held-out loss trajectory over training progress on the tested models and validation sets
reader_labels.reason: The power-law R² values are 0.6319–0.7684, below the reported temporal-law fits, and the authors state the power law is not precise enough for this temporal trajectory; see r1–r4.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Whole held-out loss trajectory over training progress on the tested models and validation sets
reader_labels.reason: The power-law fits are substantially weaker than the alternative temporal scaling fits in every reported condition, illustrating that a single power-law fit may be inadequate for these curves; see r1–r4.
